The organization, the systems, the data and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the IT support technician for Hollis and Pratt, a fictional architecture firm of 25 people in one office. Three wireless tickets arrived this week.
handover: One older access point in the reception area serves the whole office; its security is WPA2.
The plotter-printer sits on the far wall, 30 meters from the access point.
howItWorks: The desk shows the ticket queue against the priority matrix and each service's status.
Move on a day at a time. A decision comes to you at each service review; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Day 2: a shared drawing set is sent over a personal hotspot to the wrong cloud folder; a client complains.
Day 3: a stranger in the parking lot joins the open network and browses the file server.
Day 4: a contractor's laptop captures staff sign-ins from the unencrypted Wi-Fi.

roomPrompt.title: A slow meeting room
roomPrompt.context: Client calls in the meeting room keep freezing.

choices.label: Add a second access point near the meeting room, wired back to the switch, on a less crowded channel, with 5 GHz for laptops

effects.log: Calls run smoothly in the meeting room.

choices.feedback: A survey shows weak signal and crowded channels; a wired access point on a clearer channel and band fixes coverage.

choices.label: Reboot the access point every morning
choices.feedback: The signal is still weak and the channel still crowded.

choices.label: Tell staff to use their phones' hotspots for client calls
choices.feedback: Client files now cross unmanaged personal connections outside the firm's controls.

printerPrompt.title: A fixed printer far from the access point

choices.label: Run an Ethernet cable from the switch to the plotter, which never moves
choices.feedback: A fixed device far from the access point is best connected by cable.

choices.label: Add a wireless range extender near the printer
choices.feedback: Better signal, but extenders halve throughput and add another point of failure.

choices.label: Create an open network with no password next to the printer
choices.feedback: Anyone nearby can join the office network.

buyPrompt.title: Which access point to buy
buyPrompt.context: The 2014 single-band access point is due for replacement.

choices.label: Buy a current-standard dual-band access point that supports WPA3, and configure WPA3 with WPA2 fallback for older devices

effects.log: A dual-band WPA3 access point is ordered.

choices.feedback: A current dual-band access point adds the less crowded 5 GHz band, and WPA3 is the current Wi-Fi security standard.

choices.label: Buy the cheapest single-band model
choices.feedback: It repeats today's crowded 2.4 GHz problem.

choices.label: Buy a used access point that only supports open, unencrypted networks
choices.feedback: Every connection in the office would be readable over the air.

scoring.modelReasoning: Wireless problems start with a survey: weak signal and crowded channels are fixed with better placement, more access points and the less crowded band. Fixed devices belong on cables. New equipment should support current standards and security; never open the network to fix a symptom.
